description:
We are a small student team interested in software, AI, and building useful projects. We enjoy learning by building and want to use NASA Space Apps as an opportunity to work on something challenging and learn more about space and technology.

Team: Clamor
summary:
Kids read "Mars gravity is 0.38 g" and it stays a new word. In Outpost Gale they jump almost three times as high first, then the guide names it. Simulators for adults do it with manuals.

In this 3D game, a kid aged 7 to 12 commands a 2-crew base in Gale crater for 30 sols, NASA's plan for its first Mars stay. The goal is Curiosity's question, could Gale once have supported life: fly the best rock samples home.

Sols 1 to 10 are playable. Every sol goes feel, read, check, decide. PIP, the base robot, says each thing once, and every lesson lands in a handbook with a real NASA photo. Every choice costs: oxygen maker or greenhouse lamps, shelter or the day's work. Losing is never a death: Mission Control calls the crew home and shows the three costliest choices.

The ground is NASA HiRISE terrain of Gale. The Sol 5 solar storm is the one Curiosity measured on 20 May 2024. Every number traces to our 290-row fact-check table.

Built in Godot 4.7 and Blender with AI assistance (Claude). Runs in a phone browser, no login, plus Windows, Linux and macOS. Open source, Apache-2.0.
details:
We built it in Godot 4.7 with GDScript, on the Compatibility renderer so it runs in a phone browser with no login. GitHub Actions exports the Windows, Linux and macOS builds. Models came from Blender, NASA 3D Resources (the Curiosity rover) and Kenney's free kits. The ground is NASA HiRISE terrain of Gale crater, the horizon comes from NASA MOLA data, and the voices are Piper text to speech. We built it with AI assistance (Claude); the idea and the story are ours. The hardware was one laptop with integrated Intel graphics, where the game uses about 1.1 GB of memory, and a Galaxy A16 phone as the weakest test device.

It is creative because it teaches by feeling first. Simulators for adults hand you a manual. Our guide shows you the real thing, says it once, and lets you play.

We considered accuracy first: every number traces to a row in our 290-row fact-check table, and old data is labelled ARCHIVED with its date. We also considered plain words for kids, choices that always cost something, losing without fear, weak devices, slow venue Wi-Fi (the desktop builds run offline), and honest AI use.
